categories.label: Communication
categories.description: How clearly and respectfully people exchange thoughts, needs and limits.
categories.healthySignal: Messages are direct, specific and open to clarification.
categories.watchSignal: Messages are vague, dismissive or repeatedly ignored.

categories.label: Honesty
categories.description: Whether information is shared accurately and inconsistencies are addressed.
categories.healthySignal: Accounts stay consistent and gaps are owned up to.
categories.watchSignal: Stories shift, details are withheld, or accountability is avoided.

categories.label: Trust
categories.description: The degree of reliability, transparency and mutual confidence reported.
categories.healthySignal: Agreements are kept and privacy is respected.
categories.watchSignal: Agreements are broken without repair or explanation.

categories.label: Personal boundaries
categories.description: Whether stated limits about time, space, body and belongings are honoured.
categories.healthySignal: A 'no' is accepted without debate or punishment.
categories.watchSignal: Limits are pushed, tested or treated as negotiable.

categories.label: Accountability
categories.description: How mistakes, impact and repair are handled after something goes wrong.
categories.healthySignal: Impact is acknowledged and changed behaviour follows.
categories.watchSignal: Blame is shifted, harm is minimised, or 'sorry' loops repeat.

categories.label: Emotional support
categories.description: Whether feelings are met with steadiness, care and practical help.
categories.healthySignal: Distress is met with listening and useful support.
categories.watchSignal: Distress is mocked, redirected or made about someone else.

categories.label: Jealousy and control
categories.description: Attempts to monitor, restrict or direct another person's choices.
categories.healthySignal: Jealousy is named and managed without restricting freedom.
categories.watchSignal: Jealousy becomes rules, surveillance or isolation.

categories.label: Conflict resolution
categories.description: How disagreement is handled, repaired and prevented from escalating.
categories.healthySignal: Both people can raise issues and leave with a next step.
categories.watchSignal: Conflict becomes threats, silent treatment or a win/lose contest.

questions.prompt: When something bothers them, what usually happens next?
questions.hint: Think about the last few months, not one bad day.

options.label: They say it directly and stay curious
options.description: You leave the conversation understanding the issue.
options.note: Direct, curious communication is a healthy signal.

options.label: They hint, sulk or go quiet
options.description: You are left guessing what is wrong.
options.note: Indirect signals can make repair harder.

options.label: They raise it as an accusation
options.note: Accusatory openings can shut down honest exchange.

questions.prompt: When you say plans have changed, what is their first response?

options.label: They ask what works and adjust
options.description: The plan changes without a punishment phase.
options.note: Flexibility supports mutual trust.

options.label: They question your reason repeatedly
options.description: You end up defending rather than explaining.
options.note: Repeated questioning can feel like pressure.

options.label: They retaliate or withdraw affection
options.description: Changing plans comes at an emotional cost.
options.note: Using affection as leverage is a serious boundary concern.

questions.prompt: When you notice a gap in their story, what tends to follow?
questions.hint: A single fuzzy detail is different from a pattern.

options.label: They clarify and correct it
options.note: Correction without defensiveness supports reliability.

options.label: They change the subject
options.description: The gap never really gets addressed.
options.note: Topic changes can block accountability.

options.label: They insist you misremember
options.description: You start doubting your own notes.
options.note: Persistent denial of observable facts is a documented concern pattern.

questions.prompt: How do they talk about private information you shared?
questions.hint: Include what happens when you are not in the room.

options.label: They keep it private
options.description: Your trust is treated as a responsibility.
options.note: Discretion is a healthy trust signal.

options.label: They share vague hints
options.description: Enough detail that others know who you are.
options.note: Loose sharing weakens trust.

options.label: They use it in arguments
options.note: Weaponising private information is a serious boundary concern.

questions.prompt: When they say they will do something, what usually happens?
questions.hint: Think about repeated promises, not one busy week.

options.label: They follow through or communicate early
options.description: Reliability is visible in small things.
options.note: Follow-through builds dependability.

options.label: It happens eventually, after reminders
options.note: Occasional lapse; the pattern matters more than the event.

options.label: The promise quietly disappears
options.description: Nothing changes and it is not discussed.
options.note: Repeated broken agreements erode trust.

questions.prompt: How does the relationship handle time apart or other friendships?
questions.hint: Healthy trust leaves room for separate lives.

options.label: Both people keep their own lives
options.note: Autonomy and connection can coexist.

options.label: It is fine until a specific person is involved
options.description: Comfort depends on who is around.
options.note: Selective discomfort may point to unresolved insecurity.

options.label: Time apart is treated as disloyalty
options.description: Normal independence is framed as a problem.
options.note: Framing independence as disloyalty is a controlling pattern.

questions.prompt: What happens when you say no to something small?
questions.hint: Small no's reveal how larger no's will be treated.

options.label: It is accepted without comment
options.note: A respected no is a strong healthy signal.

options.label: They ask once or twice why
options.description: Curious, but they stop when you hold the line.
options.note: Clarifying questions are fine when the limit still holds.

options.label: They keep pushing until you give in
options.note: Wearing down a no is a boundary violation pattern.

questions.prompt: How are your phone, messages and personal space treated?
questions.hint: Privacy does not disappear because a relationship exists.

options.label: Each person has privacy
options.note: Respect for privacy is a healthy baseline.

options.label: They ask to look, then accept a no
options.note: Asking is different from demanding.

options.label: They check without asking or demand passwords
options.note: Unconsented monitoring is a serious privacy concern.

questions.prompt: After they hurt you, what does repair look like?
questions.hint: Look at changed behaviour, not just the apology.

options.label: They name the impact and change something
options.note: Repair includes behaviour change.

options.label: They apologise, then repeat it
options.description: The words arrive; the pattern stays.
options.note: Repeated apologies without change are a watch signal.

options.label: They say you are too sensitive
options.note: Minimising impact blocks accountability.

questions.prompt: When a mutual mistake happens, where does the blame land?
questions.hint: Notice who has to do the emotional clean-up.

options.label: Both parts are owned
options.note: Shared ownership supports fairness.

options.label: It depends on the day
options.note: Inconsistency makes repair unpredictable.

options.label: It is always your fault
options.description: You never see their part named.
options.note: Chronic blame-shifting is a documented concern pattern.

questions.prompt: When you are having a hard day, what do they do?
questions.hint: Think about the last time you were genuinely low.

options.label: Listen and ask what would help
options.note: Responsive support is a healthy signal.

options.label: Try to fix it immediately
options.description: Helpful intent, but you may feel unheard.
options.note: Support style mismatch is worth naming, not pathologising.

options.label: Mock, minimise or make it about them
options.note: Dismissing distress is a serious relational concern.

questions.prompt: How do they respond to your wins and good news?
questions.hint: Support shows up in celebration too.

options.label: They are genuinely glad
options.description: Your win is not a competition.
options.note: Shared joy is a healthy signal.

options.label: They redirect to themselves
options.note: Repeated redirecting can feel dismissive.

options.label: They undermine or compete
options.note: Undermining achievements can be a control pattern.

questions.prompt: How does jealousy show up in practice?
questions.hint: Feelings are allowed; restrictions are the thing to examine.

options.label: They name it and manage it
options.description: It becomes a conversation, not a rule.
options.note: Naming jealousy without restricting freedom is healthy.

options.label: They ask a lot of questions
options.description: It can feel tiring, but you still choose your plans.
options.note: Repeated questioning can become monitoring.

options.label: They set rules about who you see
options.description: Your choices shrink around their comfort.
options.note: Restricting contact is a controlling behaviour pattern.

questions.prompt: Can you make ordinary decisions without checking first?
questions.hint: Clothes, spending, work and plans all count.

options.label: Yes, fully
options.note: Decision autonomy is a healthy baseline.

options.label: Mostly, with some guilt
options.note: Anticipating guilt can signal an unbalanced dynamic.

options.label: No, approval is required
options.note: Requiring approval for ordinary choices is a controlling pattern.

questions.prompt: When you disagree, can you raise your side safely?
questions.hint: Safety here means emotionally, not just physically.

options.label: Yes, even when it is uncomfortable
options.description: Disagreement does not change your standing.
options.note: Being able to disagree is a strong healthy signal.

options.label: Only if the topic is small
options.note: Shrinking topics can hide unresolved issues.

options.label: No, it escalates or punishes you
options.description: You keep the real issue to yourself.
options.note: Punishment for disagreement is a serious concern.

questions.prompt: How does an argument usually end?
questions.hint: Look at what happens the next morning, not the last sentence.

options.label: With a plan or mutual understanding
options.note: A concrete repair step is a healthy sign.

options.label: It fades without resolution
options.note: Unresolved loops keep the issue alive.

options.label: With threats, silence or score-keeping
options.note: Threats and punitive silence are serious conflict concerns.
